passage: I'm Avni, and I've worked beside Wasim at the hospital lab for a year. Our shifts rotate every week: mornings, then evenings, then nights. Lately Wasim eats biscuits from the drawer instead of meals, yawns through handovers, and last Tuesday he slammed a tray down when a ward boy asked about a delayed report. That's not the Wasim I know. At tea I asked if he was all right. He rubbed his eyes and said he couldn't remember the last time he'd slept properly. I told him about the free check-up at the staff clinic, and that our supervisor once let me stay on one shift pattern for a month when I asked. He did both. I don't know how he feels inside, but he's packing lunch again.

qa.q: How often do the lab shifts rotate?
qa.a: Every week: mornings, then evenings, then nights.

qa.q: What does Wasim slamming the tray suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He seemed exhausted and short-tempered; broken sleep from the rotating shifts had worn his patience thin.

qa.q: Why were Avni's suggestions wise?
qa.a: A check-up at the staff clinic and asking the supervisor for a steadier shift pattern protect Wasim's health, since predictable hours help sleep, meals and mood.

qa.q: How might the ward boy have felt when Wasim slammed the tray?
qa.a: He was probably startled and a bit hurt, since he had only asked about a delayed report.

grounding: Shows, through a colleague's eyes, a worker whose rotating shifts disrupt sleep, meals and mood, and who is steered towards a steadier pattern and a health check-up.

passage: March: Nilesh's shifts at the textile mill flipped every few days. He ate dinner at breakfast time, dozed on the bus, and barked at his roommate Darshan for rattling a steel glass. Headaches came most afternoons, and he brushed them off with more tea. April, one Sunday: Nilesh sat down with his supervisor and asked for a steadier rotation. The supervisor agreed to longer blocks on the same shift. That week Darshan went with him to the clinic by the mill gate for a check-up; the doctor asked about sleep and meals and told him to come back if the headaches kept going or worried him. May: Nilesh cooked dal on his day off, slept at the same time most nights, and apologised to Darshan about the glass.

qa.q: What did the supervisor agree to?
qa.a: Longer blocks on the same shift.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling in March, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He was exhausted and irritable; he dozed on the bus, barked at Darshan over a rattling glass and had headaches most afternoons.

qa.q: Which choices were the turning point for Nilesh?
qa.a: Asking the supervisor for a steadier rotation and getting a check-up at the clinic, which made his sleep and meals more predictable and put his health in a doctor's view.

qa.q: What was it like for Darshan to share a room with Nilesh in March?
qa.a: Darshan was likely on edge, getting snapped at over small noises, yet still cared enough to go to the clinic with Nilesh.

grounding: Shows a worker whose changing shifts disrupt sleep, meals and mood, and how a more predictable pattern and a health check-up protect long-term wellbeing.

passage: Madhuri, I see those dark circles, so listen to an old nurse. Half this ward calls me Nandini Mausi, but at twenty-four I was a wreck. Morning shift on Monday, night on Wednesday, evening on Saturday: my body never knew when to sleep or eat. I lived on biscuits and tea, cried in the linen room, and once shouted at a patient's relative for asking a simple question. I thought that was just the job. Then my heart started fluttering, and a senior doctor made me get a proper check-up. She also helped me ask Matron for a week at a time on the same shift. I packed real meals and kept my room dark. The tiredness eased. Get yourself checked, and ask for a steadier roster, na?

qa.q: What did young Nandini live on during those shifts?
qa.a: Biscuits and tea.

qa.q: How was young Nandini feeling when she cried in the linen room?
qa.a: She felt exhausted and overwhelmed, with a body that never knew when to sleep or eat.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Nandini's story?
qa.a: The senior doctor making her get a check-up and helping her ask Matron for a week at a time on the same shift.

qa.q: How might the patient's relative have felt when Nandini shouted?
qa.a: The relative probably felt shocked and hurt, already anxious about the patient and only asking a simple question.

grounding: A senior nurse recalls how rotating shifts wrecked her sleep, meals and temper, and how a check-up and steadier roster helped.

passage: Divyansh's roster at the airport cargo bay changed every week: mornings, then nights, then evenings. This month his motorbike was also in the repair shop, so two extra hours on buses ate into his sleep. He skipped dinners, ate chips from the vending machine at three a.m., and snapped at Charu whenever she asked about weekend plans. One morning he fell asleep on the bus and woke at the depot. Charu didn't argue. She booked him a check-up at the clinic near their flat and sat with him while he wrote to his supervisor asking for two-week blocks of the same shift. The supervisor agreed to try. He started carrying packed rotis for nights.

qa.q: What did Divyansh eat at three a.m.?
qa.a: Chips from the vending machine.

qa.q: How was Divyansh feeling when he snapped at Charu?
qa.a: He was exhausted and irritable from the changing shifts and lost sleep, so small questions felt like too much.

qa.q: Which steps did Divyansh take to protect his health?
qa.a: A check-up at the clinic, asking for two-week blocks of the same shift, and carrying packed rotis for nights.

qa.q: What might Charu have felt when Divyansh kept snapping?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt and worried, but she chose to help rather than argue.

grounding: A worker on changing shifts, with a longer commute, grows exhausted and short-tempered until he gets a check-up and a steadier pattern.

passage: Nikita worked in the metro control room in Delhi, and her shifts rotated every four days. By the third month she could no longer tell whether she was hungry or tired. She ate dal-chawal at five in the morning and toast at midnight, fell asleep in her uniform, and cried over small things like a missing sock. When her flatmate Himani invited her to a friend's birthday, Nikita shouted, 'I don't have a life, okay?' and slammed her door. Later she came out and apologised. Himani said gently, 'You look exhausted all the time. Maybe see a doctor?' That week Nikita got a check-up, asked her manager for a steadier rotation, and started keeping fixed meal times.

qa.q: What did Nikita shout at Himani?
qa.a: 'I don't have a life, okay?'

qa.q: Why did Nikita cry over a missing sock?
qa.a: She was so exhausted and frazzled by the changing shifts that small things felt overwhelming.

qa.q: Which steps could protect Nikita's health in the long run?
qa.a: A doctor's check-up, a steadier rotation and fixed meal times.

qa.q: How might Himani have felt when the door slammed?
qa.a: Himani probably felt hurt and worried, yet came back gently to suggest a doctor.

grounding: A young woman on rotating shifts grows exhausted and short-tempered, and a check-up and steadier patterns protect her health.

passage:
"You've eaten breakfast at midnight three days running," Rukmini said as Nitin came in, still in his hospital scrubs.
"Rotation. Nights this week, mornings next, then evenings. My body doesn't know what day it is."
"Neither does your temper. You shouted at the cooker yesterday."
"The cooker deserved it." He sank onto the sofa. "I'm so tired my eyes hurt."
"Can you ask for the same shift for longer? Even two weeks at a time?"
"Maybe. Jaswant in my ward did."
"Then ask. And book that health check you keep postponing."
"I'm fine."
"You're grey, Nitin."
He was quiet. "Okay. I'll talk to the ward in-charge tomorrow. And book it."
"I'll come with you."

qa.q: What does Nitin's rotation look like?
qa.a: Nights this week, mornings next, then evenings.

qa.q: How is Nitin feeling after weeks of changing shifts?
qa.a: He is exhausted and short-tempered, so tired his eyes hurt, and he shouted at the cooker.

qa.q: What steps does Rukmini push Nitin to take?
qa.a: Asking for longer blocks of the same shift and booking the postponed health check.

qa.q: What is it like for Rukmini to live with Nitin's shifting hours?
qa.a: Rukmini sees the midnight breakfasts and flashes of temper and worries about Nitin's health.

grounding: Shows a worker on rotating shifts whose sleep, meals and mood are constantly disrupted, and more predictable shifts plus a health check-up as protective steps.
